idiom_name: structural interface plus a class field holding the implementation
implementation_notes: TypeScript interfaces are structural, so the letter needs no explicit implements clause: any object whose members match is assignable, and `implements` is only a compile-time check that a class satisfies the interface - it does not change the class's type. The envelope is a class or plain object holding a letter-typed property and forwarding explicitly, and swapping the letter is a property assignment. What replaces the classic structure is structural typing plus the erasure of interfaces at run time; the classic facade is still justified to publish a narrow surface and to make the compiler enforce the contract on implementors, rather than to obtain dispatch.
pitfalls: Interfaces are erased at run time, so a value that arrives from JSON, a plugin or `any` can violate the contract without any error until the method is called.
Excess property checks only apply to object literals: assigning a variable with extra members is allowed, so a letter can carry behaviour the facade never sees.

A parameter property stores the reference, so mutating the letter after construction is visible through the envelope, and `private` is compile-time only - the field is reachable from JavaScript at run time.
